value.overview: Townsend's Warbler (Setophaga townsendi) is a small North American songbird in the wood-warbler family. It breeds mainly in mature coniferous forests of western Canada and the western United States, then migrates south for winter. Its striking black, white, and yellow plumage makes it distinctive, although females and immature birds can resemble other yellow-and-black warblers. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon migrant and winter visitor rather than a breeding species.
value.classification: Order Passeriformes; family Parulidae. It is one of the Setophaga wood-warblers, a group of small insect-eating songbirds.
value.identification: Adults have a yellow face and underparts, black crown and throat markings, a dark cheek patch, and black-and-white wings. The male is more strongly marked, with a black crown, eye-line, cheek, and throat contrasting with yellow areas. Females and young birds are duller and may show less black on the head. The species commonly forages high in trees, moving actively through foliage and sometimes hovering or making short flights to capture insects.
value.rangeHabitat: Townsend's Warbler breeds from southeastern Alaska and western Canada south through the Pacific Northwest and the mountains of the western United States. During migration and winter it occurs through western Mexico and Central America, generally using mature coniferous or mixed forest, oak woodland, cloud forest, riparian vegetation, parks, gardens, and other wooded habitats. In Costa Rica it is a localized, uncommon migrant and winter visitor, most reliably associated with montane and highland forests, especially where oaks and other mature trees provide dense foliage.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. It leaves its breeding range in late summer and fall and winters from western Mexico through Central America, with Costa Rica near the southern part of its regular range. It does not normally breed in Costa Rica and is generally less numerous there than several other wintering wood-warblers.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in mature coniferous or mixed forests, especially old-growth fir, spruce, and hemlock stands with dense understory. The female usually builds a cup-shaped nest on a horizontal branch of a conifer, using bark, needles, grasses, moss, lichens, and other plant fibers, with softer material lining the interior. A clutch commonly contains three to seven eggs. Both adults feed the nestlings, and the species normally raises one brood per season.
value.dietFeeding: Townsend's Warblers feed mainly on insects and their larvae, including caterpillars, moths, beetles, ants, bees, weevils, and bugs. Spiders and small amounts of seeds or other plant material may supplement the diet. They usually glean prey from conifer needles, buds, and outer branches, but may also hover, make short aerial sallies, visit flowers for nectar during migration, or exploit sugary honeydew on wintering grounds.
value.behavior: This active foliage-gleaner often forages high in the canopy, moving quickly among leaves and branches. During the breeding season, males establish and defend territories, sometimes engaging in prolonged disputes with rivals. Pairs defend nesting and feeding areas, and both sexes help care for young. In migration and winter, Townsend's Warblers may occur alone or join mixed-species feeding flocks, including other small forest birds. Their buzzy songs are mainly heard on the breeding grounds.

conservation.populationTrend: Breeding Bird Survey information indicates a broadly stable to slightly declining population in recent decades, with regional variation.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of mature and old-growth conifer forests on the breeding grounds can reduce nesting habitat. Forest conversion and deterioration of montane and cloud forests in parts of the wintering range, including Central America, may also affect habitat quality.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature forests and maintain connected woodland, riparian, and high-elevation habitats along migration routes and in wintering areas. Support forest management that retains large conifers, native understory, and natural canopy structure, and reduce pesticide use in areas used by migrating and wintering insect-eating birds.
